The comparison that actually works is the same arithmetic for every school: take the full cost of attendance — tuition, fees, housing, food, books, travel — and subtract only the grants and scholarships. What's left is what your family is really being asked to cover that year, whether out of savings, income, or borrowing. Do that for each offer, write the numbers next to each other, and the genuinely cheapest school is frequently not the one whose letter looked most generous.
The Financial Aid article in this guide covers how to read the individual line items on an offer, and how to appeal one that doesn't work. Both are worth reading alongside this.

sections.heading: If the offer still doesn't work, an appeal is a real, legally-backed process
paragraphs: Financial aid administrators have explicit authority under federal law — the Higher Education Act's "professional judgment" provision — to adjust the figures behind your Student Aid Index when a family's real situation isn't captured by the form. A job loss after filing, new medical costs, a parent's death, unusual educational expenses: these are exactly what that authority exists for.

Two practical points most families don't know. First, the request needs documentation and specifics — dates, dollar amounts, and a plain letter explaining what changed — not just a request for more. Second, the aid administrator's decision is genuinely final: by law, neither the college president nor the Department of Education can overrule it. That's worth knowing so nobody wastes weeks escalating a decision that has nowhere to escalate to.

sections.heading: Waitlists: what they actually are, and the mistake that ends them quietly
paragraphs: A waitlist is not a soft rejection and not a maybe-in-line. It means the college found you admissible but has to see how many admitted students actually enroll by the reply deadline before it knows whether it has room. That's why waitlist movement doesn't happen until after May 1, and why it varies enormously year to year at the same school — it depends entirely on how many people said yes.

The mistake that quietly ends it: at most colleges you have to actively claim your waitlist spot through their portal, and if you don't, you're removed from consideration. Accepting a waitlist spot is free and commits you to nothing. Do it for any school you'd genuinely still attend.

⚠️ Then read that specific school's instructions before sending anything else. A letter of continued interest — a short note reaffirming that you'd enroll, plus any genuine updates since you applied — helps at many schools. But some state plainly that they will not review additional materials, and some accept updates only inside their own form with a word limit. Sending an unwanted email to a school that asked you not to is not neutral. Follow each school's stated instructions rather than generic advice about what "always" works.

sections.heading: Deferrals from an early round
paragraphs: If you applied Early Action or Early Decision and were deferred, your application moves into the regular decision pool and gets read again with that larger group. It's a different situation from a waitlist: the decision hasn't been made yet, rather than having been made conditionally.

The useful move is the same shape — a brief update with anything genuinely new since you applied (fall semester grades, a new award, a role you've taken on), sent only if that college accepts updates. And keep the rest of your applications moving on their normal schedule. A deferral is not a signal to stop applying elsewhere.

sections.heading: May 1, the deposit, and the one rule with real consequences
paragraphs: May 1 is the usual national reply date: by then, admitted students are expected to choose one college and send a deposit, which is normally non-refundable and counts toward the first tuition bill. Some colleges set different dates, and a few extend the deadline in specific circumstances — but plan around May 1 unless a school tells you otherwise in writing.

The rule worth taking seriously: deposit at exactly one school. Putting deposits down at two or more — "double depositing" — is treated across the profession as an ethics violation rather than a clever hedge, because it tells two colleges you're enrolling when you know you can only attend one. It distorts how colleges plan their class size, which directly costs a spot to someone on a waitlist. Colleges that discover it can and do rescind the admission offer.

There is one recognized exception, and it's narrow: if you're on the waitlist at a school you'd prefer and admitted somewhere else, you may deposit at the school that admitted you to secure a place while waiting. If the waitlist comes through, you withdraw from the first and forfeit that deposit. That's the intended cost of holding the option, and it's the honest version of the same move.

sections.heading: Your offer is conditional until your final transcript arrives
paragraphs: Almost every acceptance letter says, somewhere in it, that admission is contingent on successfully completing senior year. Colleges receive a final transcript after graduation, and they do read it. Grades collapsing in the final semester is the single most commonly cited reason offers get withdrawn.

This is worth stating plainly because the risk is invisible: the acceptance already arrived, so it feels finished. It isn't. Dropping a required course, failing a class, or a dramatic slide across the last semester can genuinely undo it. (National data on how often this happens is old — the main survey stopped being collected years ago — so treat the frequency as unknown and the mechanism as real.)

If something serious goes wrong academically — an illness, a family crisis, a class that fell apart — contact the admissions office yourself and explain before they find it on the transcript. A college that hears it from the student first has room to work with them. A college that discovers it in July has far less.

sections.heading: If none of it worked out
paragraphs: It happens, and it is genuinely not the end of the path. Community colleges have open admission and rolling deadlines, and — as the Community College and Transfer Pathways article covers — a planned transfer can land you at the same four-year school with the same diploma, for much less money. Many four-year colleges also still have space after May 1 and continue accepting applications; NACAC publishes a list of them every spring specifically for this situation.

A gap year with real work or responsibility, followed by applying again with a stronger application, is also a legitimate route rather than a lost year. The one thing worth avoiding is deciding in April, under pressure and disappointment, that the whole thing is over. It isn't, and the options above are ordinary rather than exceptional.

keyTerms.definition: The college's own published total for one year — tuition, fees, housing, food, books, and travel. The number to subtract grants from when comparing offers honestly.
A holding pool for admissible applicants, resolved only after the reply deadline shows the college how many admitted students actually enrolled. Usually requires actively claiming your spot.
A brief note to a college after a deferral or waitlist, confirming you'd still enroll and adding genuine updates. Welcome at many schools, explicitly unwanted at some — check each one's instructions.
An early-round outcome where no decision is made yet and the application is moved into the regular decision pool to be read again.
The normally non-refundable payment that accepts an offer of admission, typically due May 1, and credited toward the first tuition bill.

Sending enrollment deposits to more than one college. Treated as an integrity violation and grounds for rescinding admission — the narrow exception is holding a spot while on another school's waitlist.
A financial aid administrator's authority under federal law to adjust aid calculations for documented special circumstances. Their decision is final and cannot be overruled by anyone above them.
An acceptance withdrawn after the fact — most often because the final senior-year transcript showed grades that fell sharply or a required course was dropped.
